query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, uniform alumina (Al2O3) coating on equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will significantly improve its oxygen resistance at high temperatures by forming a stable passivating barrier that slows oxidation, while preserving its room- and high-temperature mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, but with inadequate oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Deposit a thin, uniform alumina (Al2O3) coating on the surface of the alloy via a suitable deposition technique (e.g., physical vapor deposition).
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at 800 °C for 5 hours; mechanical loading conditions remain similar to standard tensile test setups to ensure preservation of mechanical performance.
generation.structural_mediator: The alumina coating acts as a physical and chemical barrier, mediating oxygen diffusion into the substrate and preventing detrimental internal oxidation (pesting).
generation.mechanism: The alumina layer forms a stable, slow-growing oxide scale that adheres strongly to the substrate; this passivating barrier limits the ingress of oxygen into the underlying cast alloy, thereby mitigating pesting and maintaining the alloy’s mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated alloy will exhibit a marked reduction in oxidation (as evidenced by lower mass gain and less internal oxidation) compared to uncoated samples under identical exposure conditions, while retaining its ductility and high-temperature strength.
generation.baseline: Uncoated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, which under the same exposure conditions, shows significant oxidation leading to pesting and degradation of mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exposed to air at 800 °C for a duration of 5 hours with minimal mechanical loading; results outside these conditions may differ.
generation.uncertainty: Although similar coating strategies have improved oxidation resistance in related non-equiatomic alloys, it remains uncertain whether the same coating will perform optimally on equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr due to potential differences in substrate chemistry and coating adhesion.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr samples: one set with the applied alumina coating and one without. Expose both sets to air at 800 °C for 5 hours and then conduct a series of analyses including mass gain measurement, microstructural examination (via SEM/EDS), and mechanical tensile testing at room and high temperature.
measurements: Thickness and uniformity of the oxide scale via cross-sectional microscopy
Microstructural integrity of the coating-substrate interface
Tensile strength and ductility before and after exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alumina-coated samples display oxidation behavior (mass gain, oxide thickness, or mechanical degradation) that is statistically indistinguishable from or worse than that of the uncoated samples under the specified conditions, then the hypothesis will be falsified.
